newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania reformists take over new parliament.
newsitem.headline: Romania reformists take over new parliament.

text.p: Romania's new parliament dominated by centrists sat for the first time on Friday with ex-Communists in opposition for the first time in seven years after their election rout this month.
Defeated president Ion Iliescu sat in the Senate, the upper house housed in the former Communist Party Central Committee building.

A few kilometres (miles) away president-elect Emil Constantinescu had his election victory validated in the Chamber of Deputies, in the opulent palace built by Stalinist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu, executed after he was ousted in a bloody upheaval at the end of 1989.
Deputies queued to be photographed in marble halls the size of soccer pitches before taking their seats.
"This is a new era in Romanian history," said Constantinescu, a geology professor who defeated Iliescu in last weekend's presidential run-off.

"We cannot disappoint anybody," said Constantinescu, whose reformist Democratic Convention (CDR) bloc threw Iliescu's leftist Party of Social Democracy (PDSR) out of government in general elections earlier this month.
The centrists were still savouring their victory, which ended Romania's isolation as the only East European country still run by politicians associated with the communist past.

"After years of small steps, we now have to take big strides to secure our access to the European Union and NATO," said Valentin Gabrielescu, the oldest Senate member who opened Friday's session, devoted to procedural matters.
Constantinescu's CDR, a grouping of half a dozen parties, is linked with ex-prime minister Petre Roman's Social Democrats (USD) to form a majority in the new parliament.
Even after their defeat -- reflecting popular discontent over botched reforms and widespread poverty -- Iliescu's leftist Party of Social Democrats (PSDR) remained the largest party.

The PDSR took some 28 percent of 141 seats in the Senate and slightly less in the 343-member lower house. The Convention, led by Christian Democrats and Liberals, have 37 percent in both houses. Roman's USD have 16 percent.
On Friday, Iliescu assumed leadership of the 41-strong PDSR group in the Senate. Roman will sit as chairman, the number two state position after the president.
Talks are under way between the Convention and USD on dividing up portfolios in the government, which will also include leaders of the country's 1.6 million ethnic Hungarians.
Prime minister-designate Victor Ciorbea, the popular mayor of Bucharest, has backed Constantinescu's campaign pledges, and promised austerity will apply equally to his government.
Many deputies were awed by their lavish new hall under an ornate glass dome in the Ceausescu-era palace, where senators are also expected to move shortly.

Liberals say it is too expensive to use the building, with its 3,000 halls the world's second largest after the Pentagon in Washington. The outgoing leftists say the existing premises have been damaged by earthquakes.
Annual upkeep of the lower house in the palace costs more than $500,000, with $700,000 added on to move in the Senate.
